idiom_name: java.util.ServiceLoader on the JVM (runtime provider registry)
implementation_notes: Scala runs on the JVM, so the runtime lookup service is java.util.ServiceLoader: ServiceLoader.load(classOf[CodecFactory]) resolves providers declared in META-INF/services or module `provides` directives, instantiates them lazily and caches them, with reload() as the re-resolution hook. The Scala-idiomatic alternative is compile-time resolution: a parameter marked with `using` plus a `given` instance makes the compiler pick the binding by type, which removes the string name and the runtime failure but also removes the ability to re-resolve when the resource moves. Use the runtime registry for resources that appear, move or scale, and givens for fixed dependencies that belong to the program's configuration.
code_sketch:
import java.util.ServiceLoader

val loader = ServiceLoader.load(classOf[CodecFactory])
val it = loader.iterator()
val factory = if it.hasNext then it.next() else sys.error("no CodecFactory provider")
loader.reload()                     // drop the cache and re-resolve

// compile-time alternative:
def renderHtml(page: String)(using cfg: RenderConfig): String = s"${cfg.baseUrl}/$page"
pitfalls: A missing provider is discovered only while iterating - an empty loader is a valid registry, so applications that need a provider must fail fast explicitly.
ServiceConfigurationError is thrown lazily during iteration and is an Error, not an Exception; a catch of Exception will not see it.
Given or implicit resolution happens at compile time and cannot re-resolve at runtime, so movable resources must go through a runtime registry.

variants.name: Compile-time resolution via contextual parameters (given/using)
variants.idiom_name: contextual parameters (using) plus given instances resolved by the compiler
variants.implementation_notes: Scala's contextual abstraction replaces the lookup call with term inference: a method declares (using cfg: RenderConfig), a given instance (or an implicit definition in Scala 2) makes a canonical value available, and the compiler inserts the argument at the call site, so there is no registry lookup and no lookup failure at runtime. The trade-off is the reverse of the pattern's promise: bindings are static per scope and cannot re-resolve when a resource moves, and the chosen binding is invisible at the call site unless you read the signature. Choose it when the dependency is a program-wide configuration or capability (a clock, codec, config) rather than a movable resource; use ServiceLoader or a registry otherwise.
variants.code_sketch:
final case class RenderConfig(baseUrl: String)

given RenderConfig = RenderConfig("https://render.internal")   // binding

def renderHtml(page: String)(using cfg: RenderConfig): String =
  s"${cfg.baseUrl}/$page"

renderHtml("index")            // the compiler supplies the given instance
pitfalls: Implicit or given search can pick an unintended instance from a wildcard import or an enclosing scope; keep givens in companion objects and avoid importing foreign environments wholesale.
Resolution is compile-time, so a binding cannot be refreshed when the resource moves - dynamic configuration must use a runtime registry instead.
Two given instances of the same type make the call site ambiguous (a compile error); model alternatives with a wrapper type rather than twin givens.
